﴿By the star when it sets,﴾ Ibn ʿAbbas said, according to the narration of al-Walibi and al-ʿAwfi: it means the Pleiades (al-Thurayya) when it falls and disappears, and its "hawi" (falling) is its setting. The Arabs call the Pleiades a "najm" (star).

It has come in a hadith from Abu Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him), traced to the Prophet (ﷺ): "Whenever the star rises, no blight remains on the earth without being lifted." [Imam Ahmad narrated it: 2/341 and 2/388, with the wording: "When the star rises in the morning, blight is lifted." al-Suyuti marked it as hasan in al-Jami al-Saghir (5/454) with Fayd al-Qadir. Al-Haythami said in Majma al-Zawa'id: 4/103, "All of it was narrated by Ahmad, and al-Tabarani in al-Saghir with the wording: 'When the star rises, blight is lifted from every land,' and similarly in al-Awsat. In its chain is ʿAsal ibn Safwan: Ibn Hibban declared him reliable but said he errs and contradicts others, and a group weakened him; the rest of its narrators are those of the sahih."] It was also narrated by Imam Muhammad ibn al-Hasan al-Shaybani, with a chain whose narrators are trustworthy, in Kitab al-Athar, page 159; and by al-Tahawi in Mushkil al-Athar (3/91). Ibn ʿAdi narrated it in al-Kamil: 7/2478. See also: Mushkil al-Athar 3/92; Sharh Musnad Abi Hanifah by Mulla ʿAli al-Qari, page 141; Silsilat al-Ahadith al-Da'ifah by al-Albani: 1/389-390. By "the star" he meant the Pleiades.

Mujahid said: it refers to all the stars of the sky when they set. The word is singular but its meaning is plural. The celestial body was called "najm" because of its rising (tuluʿ), and every rising thing is a "najm." It is said: "najama al-sinn, al-qarn, wa-al-nabt" (the tooth, horn, and plant emerged) when it rose.

ʿIkrimah narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas that it refers to the meteors among the stars, meaning what the devils are struck with when they eavesdrop.

Abu Hamzah al-Thumali said: it refers to the stars when they scatter on the Day of Resurrection. It was also said: the intended "najm" is the Qur'an, and it was called "najm" because it was revealed in separate portions over twenty years. Dispersing it is called "tanjim," and what is dispersed is called "munajjam." This is the view of Ibn ʿAbbas in the narration of ʿAta', and it is the view of al-Kalbi.

"Al-hawi" means descending from a high place to a low place. Al-Akhfash said: "al-najm" is the plant that has no stalk, and from it is the saying of the Mighty and Majestic: ﴿And the star and the tree prostrate﴾ [al-Rahman: 6], and its "hawi" is its falling onto the ground. Ja'far al-Sadiq said: it means Muhammad (ﷺ) when he descended from the sky on the night of the Ascension (al-Mi'raj). "Al-hawi" is descent; it is said: "hawa yahwi hawiyyan" [when he descended], like "mada yamdi mudiyyan."

In most Arabic speech, when they want to join two subjects in such a construction, they make the pronoun of the first-mentioned subject explicit, saying "istawa huwa wa-fulan" (he and so-and-so stood). The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) asked him to show him himself in the form in which he was created, so he showed him himself twice: once on earth and once in the heavens. As for on earth, it was at the highest horizon, and by "the highest" is meant the eastern side. This is because Muhammad (ﷺ) was in Hira', and Jibril appeared to him from the east and filled the horizon to the west, so the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) fell unconscious. Commentary of al-Baghawi (Ma'alim al-Tanzil) on surah 53, verses 8–9:

His words, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿Then he approached and descended, and was at a distance of two bow-lengths or nearer﴾. The scholars differed concerning its meaning.

Abd al-Wahid al-Malihi informed us, Ahmad ibn Abd Allah al-Nu'aymi informed us, Muhammad ibn Yusuf informed us, Muhammad ibn Isma'il (al-Bukhari) narrated to us, Abu Usama narrated to us, Zakariyya ibn Abi Za'ida narrated to us, from Ibn al-Ash'a, from al-Sha'bi, from Masruq, who said: I said to Aisha: "Then what about His saying: ﴿Then he approached and descended, and was at a distance of two bow-lengths or nearer﴾?" She said: "That was Jibril. He used to come to him in the form of a man, but this time he came to him in his own form, and he filled the horizon."[[Narrated by al-Bukhari in Bad' al-Khalq, chapter "When one of you says 'Amin' and the angels in the heaven say it too, and their saying coincides, his previous sins are forgiven": 6/313.]]

Abd al-Wahid al-Malihi informed us, Ahmad ibn Abd Allah al-Nu'aymi informed us, Muhammad ibn Yusuf informed us, Muhammad ibn Isma'il narrated to us, Talq ibn Ghannam narrated to us, Za'ida narrated to us, from al-Shaybani, who said: I asked Zirr about His saying: ﴿and was at a distance of two bow-lengths or nearer﴾. He said: Abd Allah (meaning Ibn Mas'ud) informed us that Muhammad ﷺ saw Jibril, who had six hundred wings.[[Narrated by al-Bukhari in Tafsir, Surat al-Najm, chapter "Then He revealed to His servant what He revealed" (53:10): 8/610, and in Bad' al-Khalq: 6/313.]]

So the meaning of the verse is: Then Jibril approached after he had become level with the highest horizon of the earth, "and descended", and came down to Muhammad ﷺ, so that there was between them "a distance of two bow-lengths or nearer", indeed nearer. This is the view of Ibn Abbas, al-Hasan and Qatada. It has been said: there is inversion in the speech, its meaning being: "Then he descended and approached", because descent is the cause of approach.[[See: al-Asma' wa'l-Sifat of al-Bayhaqi: 2/187-188; Ma'ani al-Qur'an of al-Farra': 3/95-96.]]

Others said: Then the Lord, Mighty and Majestic, approached Muhammad ﷺ and descended, and drew near to him until He was at a distance of two bow-lengths or nearer. It has been narrated in the account of the Mi'raj, from Sharik ibn Abd Allah, from Anas: "And the Almighty, the Lord of Might, drew near and descended, until He was at a distance of two bow-lengths or nearer."[[For what the scholars said about the narration of Sharik ibn Abd Allah and his errors in the wording of the hadith of the Mi'raj, see: Fath al-Bari, Kitab al-Tawhid, chapter on the saying of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, "And Allah spoke to Musa directly": 13/478-480; Ibn Kathir: 4/250; al-Asma' wa'l-Sifat of al-Bayhaqi: 2/187.]] This is the narration of Ibn Salama from Ibn Abbas. "Tadalli" (descending) is coming down to a thing until it draws near to it.

Mujahid said: Jibril approached his Lord.[[See: al-Asma' wa'l-Sifat: 2/188.]]

Al-Dahhak said: Muhammad ﷺ approached his Lord and descended, and he bowed down in prostration, and so there was between them a distance of two bow-lengths or nearer.

The meaning of His saying "qaba qawsayn" is: the measure of two bows. "Al-qab", "al-qayb", "al-qad" and "al-qayd" are all expressions for a measure. "Al-qaws" (the bow) is that by which arrows are shot, according to the statement of al-Dahhak, Mujahid, Ikrima and Ata, from Ibn Abbas. So He informed that the distance between Jibril and Muhammad, peace be upon them both, was the measure of two bows. Mujahid said: its meaning is "where the string is on the bow", and this is an indication of emphasizing the nearness. Its origin: when two allies among the Arabs wished to establish friendship and covenant, they would go out with their two bows and press them together between them, intending by that that they were mutually supporting, each defending the other.

Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud said: "qaba qawsayn" means: the measure of two cubits. This is also the view of Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Shaqiq ibn Salama. "Al-qaws" is the cubit, by which everything is measured. "Aw adna" means: rather, nearer.

The others read it with a single *dhal* (*takhfif*), meaning: the heart of Muhammad (ﷺ) did not lie about what it saw; rather, it spoke the truth. It is said: "kadhdhabahu" (he called him a liar) when one tells him a lie. Its sense is: the heart did not lie concerning what it saw.

Abd al-Wahid al-Malihi informed us, Ahmad ibn 'Abdullah al-Nu'aymi informed us, Muhammad ibn Yusuf informed us, Muhammad ibn Isma'il narrated to us, Yahya narrated to us, Waki' narrated to us, from Isma'il ibn Abi Khalid, from 'Amir, from Masruq, who said: I said to 'A'ishah, "O mother, did Muhammad (ﷺ) see his Lord?" "Whoever tells you that he knows what will happen tomorrow has lied." Then she recited: "﴿And no soul knows what it will earn tomorrow﴾" [Luqman: 34]. "Whoever tells you that he concealed something has lied." Then she recited: "﴿O Messenger, convey what has been revealed to you from your Lord﴾" [al-Ma'idah: 67], to the end of the verse. **Commentary of al-Baghawi (Ma'alim al-Tanzil) on Surah 53, verses 12–14:**

﴿Will you then dispute with him about what he sees?﴾ Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Ya'qub read "أَفَتَمْرُونَهُ" (*afatamrunahu*) with a fatha on the *ta'* and a sukun on the *mim* [[Addition from manuscript "ب".]], without an alif, meaning: "Will you then deny him?" The Arabs say: "*maraytu al-rajula haqqahu*" ("I denied the man his right") when one denies him what is due. The others read "أَفَتُمَارُونَهُ" (*afatumarunahu*) with an alif and a damma on the *ta'*, meaning: "Will you then argue with him about what he sees?" This is because they argued with him when he was taken on the Night Journey (*Isra'*). They said: "Describe Bayt al-Maqdis to us, and tell us about our caravan on the way," and other things with which they argued against him. The meaning is: "Will you argue with him in a way by which you intend to repel what he saw and knew?"

﴿And he certainly saw him in another descent,﴾ meaning: he saw Jibril in his original form, in which he was created, descending from the sky in another descent. This was because he saw him in his form twice: once on the earth and once in the sky.

﴿at the Lote-tree of the Utmost Boundary.﴾ According to the opinion of Ibn Abbas, the meaning of "another descent" is that the Prophet ﷺ had ascents (*'arajat*) on that night for the matter of reducing the number of prayers. So each ascent had a descent, and he saw his Lord during some of them. It has been related from him: "He saw his Lord with his heart (*fu'ad*) twice" [[Narrated by Muslim in al-Iman, chapter on the meaning of Allah's words, "And he certainly saw him in another descent" (*wa-laqad ra'ahu nazlatan ukhra*), no. 176: 1/158.]], and from him also: "He saw with his eyes" [[Ibn Kathir cited the narration of Imam Ahmad from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both: "I saw my Lord, Mighty and Majestic," and said: "Its chain is according to the conditions of the sahih, but it is an abridgement of a hadith about a dream": 4/252. Then he said on the following page: "It has been mentioned that Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, affirmed the vision on the night of the Isra', and cited this verse, 'And he certainly saw him in another descent.' A group of the early and later scholars followed him, but groups of the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, and the Successors and others opposed him."]].

As for His words, "at the Lote-tree of the Utmost Boundary": it has been related from Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, who said: When the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was taken on the Night Journey, he reached the Lote-tree of the Utmost Boundary, which is in the seventh heaven. To it ends what ascends from the earth, and it is taken from there; and to it ends what descends from above it, and it is taken from there. Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿Near it is the Garden of Refuge, when there covered the Lote-tree that which covers﴾. He said: "[It is covered by] a carpet of gold" [[Narrated by Muslim in al-Iman, chapter on mentioning the Lote-tree of the Utmost Boundary, no. 173: 1/157.]].

And it has been related in the hadith of the Mi'raj: "Then I was taken up to the seventh heaven, and there I found Ibrahim, peace be upon him, and I greeted him. Then the Lote-tree of the Utmost Boundary was raised for me, and its fruits were like the jars of Hajar, and its leaves were like the ears of elephants" [[A portion of the hadith of Malik ibn Sa'sa'ah, may Allah be pleased with him, concerning the Mi'raj, narrated by al-Bukhari in Bad' al-Khalq, chapter on mentioning the angels: 6/302–303, and by Muslim in al-Iman, chapter on the Night Journey of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ to the heavens and the obligation of the prayers, no. 162: 1/145–147.]].

"Al-Sidrah" is the lote-tree (*shajarat al-nabq*). It was called "Lote-tree of the Utmost Boundary" because the knowledge of creation ends at it. Hilal ibn Yasaf said: Ibn Abbas asked Ka'b about the Lote-tree of the Utmost Boundary while I was present. Ka'b said: "It is a lote-tree at the base of the Throne, upon the heads of the bearers of the Throne, and to it ends the knowledge of creatures; and what is beyond it is unseen, which none knows except Allah" [[Attributed by al-Suyuti in al-Durr al-Manthur: 7/650 to Ibn Abi Shaybah.]].

Abu Sa'id al-Shurayhi informed us, Abu Ishaq al-Tha'labi informed us, Ibn Fanjawayh informed me, Ibn Shaybah related to us, al-Masuhi related to us, Ubayd ibn Ya'ish related to us, Yunus ibn Bukayr related to us, Muhammad ibn Ishaq informed us from Yahya ibn Abbad ibn Abdullah ibn al-Zubayr, from his father, from his grandmother Asma' bint Abi Bakr, who said: I heard the Prophet ﷺ mention the Lote-tree of the Utmost Boundary, and he said: "A rider travels in the shade of one of its branches for a hundred years, and a hundred thousand riders can shelter in its branches. In it is a carpet of gold, and its fruit is like jars" [[Narrated by al-Tirmidhi in Sifat al-Jannah, chapter on what has come concerning the description of the fruits of Paradise: 7/248–249, who said: "This is a hasan sahih gharib hadith"; and al-Tabari: 27/54–55; and al-Hakim: 2/469, who said: "This is a sahih hadith according to the conditions of Muslim, though they did not narrate it." al-Suyuti in al-Durr al-Manthur: 7/650 added its attribution to Ibn Mardawayh.]].

Muqatil said: It is a tree that bears ornaments, garments and fruits of all colours. If a single leaf of it were placed on the earth, it would illuminate the people of the earth. It is the *Tuba* that Allah, the Exalted, mentioned in Surah al-Ra'd.

Commentary of al-Baghawi (Ma'alim al-Tanzil) on surah 53, verses 15–18:

﴿Near it is the Garden of Refuge﴾. ʿAṭāʾ reported from Ibn ʿAbbās: "It is a garden to which Jibrīl and the angels retreat." Muqātil and al-Kalbī said: "To it the spirits of the martyrs retreat."

It has been related in the hadith of the Mi'raj (Ascension) from Anas, from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "Then I was taken to the Lote-Tree of the Utmost Boundary. Its leaves were like the ears of elephants and its fruits like large water-jars. When there covered it some of the command of Allah that covered it, it changed, and no one of Allah's creation is able to describe its beauty. Then He revealed to me what He revealed, and He prescribed upon me fifty prayers each day and night." [[A portion of a hadith narrated by Muslim in al-Iman, chapter on the Night Journey of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)... no. 162: 1/145–146.]]

Muqātil said: "The angels cover it like crows." al-Suddī said: "Like birds." It was narrated from Abū al-ʿĀliyah, from Abū Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him), or from another, who said: "The light of creation covered it, and the angels covered it out of love for Allah, like crows when they alight upon a tree." He said: "Then He spoke to him at that moment, and said to him: 'Ask.'" [[Narrated by al-Ṭabarī: 27/56; see also Ibn Kathīr's Tafsir: 4/253.]] From al-Ḥasan, who said: "The light of the Lord of Might covered it, and it became radiant." It is also reported in a hadith: "I saw upon every leaf of it an angel standing, glorifying Allah, exalted is He." [[Narrated by al-Ṭabarī: 27/56.]]

﴿The sight did not swerve, nor did it transgress﴾. That is: the eye of the Prophet (ﷺ) did not turn to the right or to the left, "nor did it transgress," that is, it did not go beyond what it saw. It was also said: it did not go beyond what he was commanded. This describes his good manners in that station, for he did not turn to one side.

Commentary of al-Baghawi (Ma'alim al-Tanzil) on surah 53, verse 19:

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿Have you considered al-Lat and al-'Uzza?﴾ These are the names of idols which they took as gods and worshipped. They derived names for them from the names of God Most High: from Allah they said "al-Lat," and from al-'Aziz (the Mighty) they said "al-'Uzza." It is also said that al-'Uzza is the feminine form of al-A'azz (the Mightiest). As for "al-Lat," Qatadah said: it was at al-Ta'if. Ibn Zayd said: it was a house at Nakhlah which the Quraysh used to worship. [Al-Tabari mentioned these two opinions: 27/58-59.]

Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and Abu Salih read "al-Lattu" (ال    لاتّ) with a doubled ta' (shaddah), and they said: he was a man who used to knead sawiq (a porridge of roasted grain) for the pilgrims. When he died, they devoted themselves to his grave, worshipping him. [Al-Bukhari recorded it in the Tafsir, Surat al-Najm, chapter: "Have you considered al-Lat and al-'Uzza": 8/611, first narration: "al-Lat was a man who kneaded sawiq for the pilgrims."]

Mujahid said: he was on the top of a mountain, where he had a small flock of goats. He would churn ghee from their milk, take curds from it, and gather their milk (ristl, meaning milk), then make from it a hays (a dish of dates, butter and curds) and feed the pilgrims with it. He was in the valley of Nakhlah. When he died, they worshipped him, and he is al-Lat. [Al-Suyuti attributed it in al-Durr al-Manthur: 7/653 to Sa'id ibn Mansur and al-Fakihi.]

Al-Kalbi said: he was a man from Thaqif called Sirmah ibn Ghanm, who used to churn ghee and place it on a rock, and the Arabs would come to him and knead their sawiq with it. When the man died, Thaqif moved it to their dwellings and worshipped it. So the lote-tree of al-Ta'if stands on the site of al-Lat.

As for "al-'Uzza": Mujahid said: it was a tree belonging to Ghatafan, which they worshipped. So the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) sent Khalid ibn al-Walid, who cut it down. Khalid ibn al-Walid began striking it with an axe and saying:

"O 'Uzza, disbelieve in you! Not glorified are you!
Indeed I have seen that Allah has humiliated you!"

Then there came out from it a female devil, her hair loose, calling out "Woe!" and placing her hand on her head.

It is also said that Khalid returned to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: "I have uprooted it." He said: "What did you see?" He said: "I saw nothing." The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "You have not uprooted it; go back to it." So he returned to it with the pickaxe, uprooted it and tore out its root, and a naked woman came out of it, and he killed her. Then he returned to the Prophet (ﷺ) and informed him of that. He said: "That was al-'Uzza, and she will never be worshipped again." [Sahib al-Fath al-Samawi attributed it in 3/907 to Ibn Mardawayh.]

Al-Dahhak said: it was an idol of Ghatafan, which Sa'd ibn Zalim al-Ghatafani set up for them, because he came to Makkah and saw al-Safa and al-Marwah, and saw the people of Makkah circling between them. He returned to the valley of Nakhlah and said to his people: "The people of Makkah have al-Safa and al-Marwah, and these are not yours, and they have a god which they worship and you do not have." They said: "What do you command us?" He said: "I will make one for you like that." So he took a stone from al-Safa and a stone from al-Marwah and carried them to Nakhlah. He placed the one he had taken from al-Safa and said: "This is al-Safa." Then he placed the one he had taken from al-Marwah and said: "This is al-Marwah." Then he took three stones and propped them against a tree and said: "This is your lord." So they began circling between the two stones and worshipping the stones, until the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) conquered Makkah. He ordered the stones removed, and sent Khalid ibn al-Walid to al-'Uzza, and he cut it down.

Ibn Zayd said: it is a house at al-Ta'if which Thaqif used to worship.

**﴿And Manat﴾** Ibn Kathir recited it with a long vowel and a hamza (*Manā'a*), while the majority of readers (*al-'āmma*) recited it with a short vowel and without a hamza (*Manat*). The reason is that the Arabs named people Zayd Manat and 'Abd Manat, and no long-vowel form was heard in those names. Qatadah said: it belonged to Khuza'ah and was at Qudayd. 'A'ishah, may Allah be pleased with her, said regarding the Ansar: "They used to chant the talbiyah for Manat, and it was opposite Qudayd." Ibn Zayd said: it was a house at al-Mushallal, worshipped by the Banu Ka'b. al-Dahhak said: Manat was an idol of Hudhayl and Khuza'ah, which the people of Makkah worshipped. Some said: al-Lat, al-'Uzza and Manat were idols made of stone that were inside the Ka'bah, and they worshipped them.[[Some of these statements are mentioned by al-Tabari (27/59–60), al-Bahr al-Muhit (8/161), and Zad al-Masir (8/72). Then the author of al-Bahr al-Muhit (8/161), after mentioning what was said about the locations of these idols, said: "This is considerable confusion regarding these idols and their locations, and what appears is that all three were in the Ka'bah, because the one addressed in His words ﴿Have you considered?﴾ is the Quraysh."]]

The readers (*qurra'*) differed on the pause (*waqf*) at **al-Lat** and **Manat**: some paused on them with a *ha'* (ـه), and some with a *ta'* (ـت). Some said: what is written in the *mushaf* (the written codex) with a *ta'* is paused on with a *ta'*, and what is written with a *ha'* is paused on with a *ha'*.

As for His words **﴿the third, the other﴾**: "the third" is an attribute (*na't*) of Manat, meaning the third of the two idols mentioned. As for "the other," the Arabs do not say "the third, the other"; rather, "the other" here is an attribute of "the second." Al-Khalil said: the *ya'* (in *ukhrā*, feminine form) is for the sake of agreement with the verse endings (*ru'ūs al-āy*), as in His words ﴿other uses﴾ [Ta-Ha: 18], where He did not say *ukhar*. It was also said: there is inversion (*taqdīm wa ta'khīr*) in the verse, its intended meaning being: "Have you considered al-Lat and al-'Uzza the other, and Manat the third?"

The meaning of the verse: **"Have you considered?"** means: tell us, O you who claim that al-Lat, al-'Uzza and Manat are daughters of Allah. al-Kalbi said: the polytheists in Makkah used to say, "The idols and the angels are the daughters of Allah." When one of them was given the good news of a female child, he would dislike it.

Commentary of al-Baghawi (Ma'alim al-Tanzil) on surah 53, verses 21–23:

Then Allah Most High said, rebuking them: ﴿Is the male for you and the female for Him? That, then, would be an unfair division.﴾ Ibn 'Abbas and Qatadah said: that is, an unjust division, since you have assigned to your Lord what you dislike for yourselves. Mujahid and Muqatil said: a crooked division. Al-Hasan said: not balanced.

Ibn Kathir recited "ḍi'zā" with a hamzah, while the others recited it without hamzah.

Al-Kisa'i said: From this one says ḍāza yaḍīzu ḍaydhan, and ḍāza yaḍūzu ḍawdhan, and ḍāza yuḍāzu ḍāzan, meaning he wronged and diminished. The form of ḍīzā in speech is fu'lā with the fa' vowelled with a ḍammah, because it is an adjective, and adjectives are only of the pattern fu'lā with a ḍammah on the fa', like ḥubla (pregnant), unthā (female) and bushrā (good tidings), or fa'lā with a fatḥah on the fa', like ghaḍbā (angry), sakrā (intoxicated) and 'aṭshā (thirsty). There is no fi'lā with a kasrah on the fa' among the adjectives in the speech of the Arabs; it occurs only in nouns, such as dhikrā and shi'rā. The kasrah of the ḍād here is so that the yā' is not converted into a wāw, while it is from the roots of yā', as they said in the plural of abyaḍ, bīḍ, whereas the original is būḍ, like ḥumr and ṣufr. As for the one who says ḍāza yaḍūzu, the noun from it is ḍūzā, like shūrā.

﴿They are but names that you and your fathers have named, for which Allah has sent down no authority.﴾ That is, these idols are only names, with no proof for your claim that they are gods. Then he turned from address back to narration, saying: ﴿They follow only conjecture﴾ in their saying that they are gods, ﴿and what their souls desire﴾ and what Satan has made attractive to them. ﴿And there has certainly come to them from their Lord guidance﴾ — the clarification through the Book and the Messenger that they are not gods, since worship is fitting only for Allah, the One, the Subduer.

﴿They are but names that you and your fathers have named, for which Allah has sent down no authority.﴾ That is, these idols are only names, with no proof for your claim that they are gods. The root meaning of "al-lamam" and "al-ilmam" is what a person does from time to time, which does not become a constant repetition or a settled practice.

Then they differed about its meaning. Some of them said: it is what occurred in the Jahiliyyah, so Allah does not hold them accountable for it. This is because the polytheists said to the Muslims: "Were you not doing these things with us only yesterday?" So Allah revealed this verse. This is the view of Zayd ibn Thabit and Zayd ibn Aslam. [[Mentioned by al-Tabari: 27/64 from Ibn Zayd. Others said: it is the minor sins, such as a glance, a squeeze, a kiss, and whatever falls short of fornication. This is the view of Ibn Mas'ud, Abu Hurayrah, Masruq, al-Sha'bi, and a narration of Tawus from Ibn 'Abbas. [[See: Zad al-Masir: 8/76.]]

'Abd al-Wahid al-Maliyhi informed us: Ahmad ibn 'Abdullah al-Nu'aymi informed us: Muhammad ibn Yusuf informed us: Muhammad ibn Isma'il informed us: Mahmud ibn Ghaylan informed us: 'Abd al-Razzaq informed us: Ma'mar informed us, from Ibn Tawus, from his father, from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "I have not seen anything more similar to al-lamam than what Abu Hurayrah narrated from the Prophet ﷺ: 'Indeed Allah has written for the son of Adam his share of adultery, which he will inevitably encounter. [[Narrated by Muslim in al-Qadar, chapter "Allah has decreed for the son of Adam his share of adultery and other things," no. (2657): 4/2047.]]

Commentary of al-Baghawi (Ma'alim al-Tanzil) on surah 53, verse 33:

His saying, exalted and majestic is He: ﴿Have you seen the one who turned away?﴾ It was revealed concerning al-Walid ibn al-Mughira. **Commentary of al-Baghawi (Ma'alim al-Tanzil) on surah 53, verses 34–37:**

So that is His saying: "And gave a little and withheld," i.e., he did not believe in him. The meaning of "*akda*" is "cut off." Its origin is from *al-kudya*, which is a rock that appears in a well and prevents digging. The Arabs say: "*akda al-hafir*" and "*ajbal*," when the digger reaches the *kudya* and the mountain (solid rock) during digging [[In the places mentioned above.]].

﴿Has he knowledge of the unseen, so that he sees⁠﴾ what is hidden from him, and knows that his companion will bear his punishment?

﴿Or has he not been informed⁠﴾, i.e., not told ﴿of what is in the scrolls of Musa⁠﴾, meaning: the books of the Torah.

﴿And Ibrahim⁠﴾ — in the scrolls of Ibrahim, peace be upon him — ﴿who fulfilled⁠﴾, i.e., completed and perfected what he was commanded.

Al-Hasan, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, and Qatadah said: He acted upon what he was commanded and conveyed the messages of his Lord to His creation [[Mentioned by al-Tabari: 27/72. See also: Ibn Kathir: 4/258; al-Bahr al-Muhit: 8/167; al-Qurtubi: 17/113.]].

Al-Rabi' said: He fulfilled his vision and undertook to slaughter his son [[Mentioned by the author of al-Bahr al-Muhit: 8/167.]].

'Ata al-Khurasani said: He completed obedience. Abu al-'Aliyah said: He fulfilled the portions of Islam. This is His saying: "And when Ibrahim was tested by his Lord with words, and he fulfilled them" [al-Baqarah: 124]. And *al-tawfiyah* means completion. Abu Ahmad ibn 'Abd Allah al-Salihi related to us: Abu Bakr Ahmad ibn al-Hasan al-Khayri related to us: Abu Ja'far Muhammad ibn 'Ali ibn Duhaym al-Shaybani related to us: Ibrahim ibn Ishaq al-Zuhri related to us: Ishaq ibn Mansur related to us, from Isra'il, from Ja'far ibn al-Zubayr, from al-Qasim, from Abu Umamah, from the Prophet ﷺ, who said: "Ibrahim, who fulfilled [prayed] four rak'ahs at the beginning of the day"[[Omitted from manuscript "b".]] [[Narrated by al-Tabari: 27/73. Ibn Kathir said: "Ibn Jarir narrated it from the hadith of Ja'far ibn al-Zubayr, and he is weak" (4/259). Al-Suyuti also attributed it in al-Durr al-Manthur (7/660) to Sa'id ibn Mansur and 'Abd ibn Humayd.]].

Abu 'Uthman al-Dabbi related to us: Abu Muhammad al-Jirahi related to us: Abu al-'Abbas al-Mahbubi related to us: Abu 'Isa al-Tirmidhi related to us: Abu Ja'far al-Shaybani related to us: Abu Mis'har related to us: Isma'il ibn 'Ayyash related to us, from Buhayr ibn Sa'd, from Khalid ibn Ma'dan, from Jubayr ibn Nufayr, from Abu al-Darda' and Abu Dharr, from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, from Allah, Blessed and Exalted, that He said: "Son of Adam, perform four rak'ahs for Me at the beginning of the day, and I will suffice you for its end" [[Narrated by al-Tirmidhi in al-Witr, chapter on what has come regarding the Duha prayer: 2/585; Abu 'Isa said: "This is a strange (gharib) hadith." Abu Dawud also narrated it in al-Tatawwu' (2/85) from Nu'aym ibn Hammar. Al-Mundhiri said: "Al-Tirmidhi narrated it from the hadith of Abu al-Darda' and Abu Dharr, and said: 'hasan gharib,' this is the end of his words. It is known from al-Mundhiri's words that the copy of al-Tirmidhi he had read: "This is a hasan gharib hadith." See: Tuhfat al-Ahwadhi: 2/585–586. Imam Ahmad also narrated it: 5/286 from Nu'aym ibn Hammar al-Ghatafani.]].

Then He explained what is in their scrolls, saying: ﴿That no bearer of burdens shall bear the burden of another﴾. In this is a refutation of the view of those who guaranteed to al-Walid ibn al-Mughira that he would bear his sin for him.

And ʿIkrima narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: Before Ibrahim (peace be upon him), they used to hold a man accountable for the sin of another. A man would be killed for the killing committed by his father, his son, his brother, his wife, or his slave, until Ibrahim (peace be upon him) came and forbade them from that, and conveyed to them from Allah: "That no bearer of burdens shall bear the burden of another."

Commentary of al-Baghawi (Ma'alim al-Tanzil) on surah 53, verse 43–47:

﴿And that it is He who causes laughter and causes weeping﴾. This indicates that everything a person does is by His decree and creation, even laughing and weeping. Mujahid and al-Kalbi said: "He caused the people of Paradise to laugh in Paradise, and caused the people of the Fire to weep in the Fire." Al-Dahhak said: "He caused the earth to laugh with vegetation, and caused the sky to weep with rain."

ʿAtaʾ ibn Abi Muslim said: "It means He makes [one] rejoice and makes [one] grieve, because joy brings laughter and grief brings weeping."

Abd al-Wahid ibn Ahmad al-Malihi informed us, Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Shurayh informed us, Abu al-Qasim al-Baghawi informed us, Ali ibn al-Ja'd related to us, Qays, that is Ibn al-Rabi al-Asadi, informed us, Simak ibn Harb related to us, who said: I said to Jabir ibn Samura: "Did you use to sit with the Prophet (ﷺ)?" He said: "Yes, and his companions would sit and recite poetry to one another, and mention things from the time of ignorance, and they would laugh, and he would smile with them when they laughed." [[Narrated by al-Tirmidhi in al-Adab, chapter on what has come concerning the recitation of poetry: 8/142-143, and he said: "This is a hasan sahih hadith", and Imam Ahmad: 5/91. Muslim narrated it in al-Fada'il, chapter on his (ﷺ) smiling and his good companionship, no. (2322): 4/1810, with the wording: "Did you sit with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)? He said: Yes, often. Ma'mar related from Qatadah: Ibn Umar was asked, "Did the companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) laugh?" He said: "Yes, and faith in their hearts was greater than a mountain." [[Narrated by Abd al-Razzaq in al-Musannaf: 11/451.]]

﴿And that upon Him is the other creation﴾. That is, the second creation for resurrection on the Day of Judgment.

Commentary of al-Baghawi (Ma'alim al-Tanzil) on surah 53, verses 61–62:

﴿And you are proud⁠—﴾ heedless and negligent. And "al-sumud" (heedlessness, distraction): being unmindful of something and being diverted. It is said: "Leave your sumud," meaning your amusement. This is the narration of al-Walibi and al-Awfi from Ibn Abbas [[See: al-Durr al-Manthur: 7/667.]]. Ikrimah said on his authority: it is singing in the dialect of the people of Yemen, for when they heard the Qur'an they would sing and play. [[Narrated by al-Tabari: 27/82, and al-Suyuti attributed it in al-Durr al-Manthur: 7/667 to Sa'id ibn Mansur and Abd ibn Humayd.]] Al-Dahhak said: "Insolent and wanton." Mujahid said: "Angry and turning away [mubarti'un]." It was asked of him: "What is al-bartama?" He said: "Turning away." [[Narrated by al-Tabari: 27/82, and al-Suyuti attributed it in al-Durr al-Manthur: 7/667 to Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn al-Mundhir.]]

﴿So prostrate to Allah and worship [Him].﴾ That is: and worship Him.

Abd al-Wahid al-Maliki informed us, Ahmad ibn Abd Allah al-Nu'aymi informed us, Muhammad ibn Yusuf informed us, Muhammad ibn Isma'il narrated to us, Musaddad narrated to us, Abd al-Warith narrated to us, Ayyub narrated to us from Ikrimah from Ibn Abbas that the Prophet (ﷺ) prostrated during [the recitation of] al-Najm, and the Muslims, the polytheists, the jinn and mankind prostrated with him. [[Narrated by al-Bukhari in the chapter on prostration during Qur'an recitation, "the prostration of Muslims with polytheists": 2/553, and in the commentary of Surah al-Najm: 8/614, and by the author in Sharh al-Sunnah: 3/301.]]

Abd al-Wahid al-Maliki informed us, Ahmad ibn Abd Allah al-Nu'aymi informed us, Muhammad ibn Yusuf informed us, Muhammad ibn Isma'il informed us, Nasr ibn Ali narrated to us, Abu Ahmad informed me, Isra'il narrated to us from Abu Ishaq from al-Aswad ibn Yazid from Abd Allah, who said: The first surah in which a prostration was revealed was al-Najm. He said: So the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) prostrated, and those behind him prostrated, except a man whom I saw take a handful of dust and prostrate upon it. I later saw him killed as a disbeliever, and he was Umayyah ibn Khalaf. [[Narrated by al-Bukhari in the commentary, Surah al-Najm, chapter "So prostrate to Allah and worship": 8/614, the wording being his, and by Muslim in the book of mosques, chapter on prostration of recitation, no. (576): 1/405.]]

And Abd al-Wahid al-Maliki informed us, Ahmad ibn Abd Allah al-Nu'aymi informed us, Muhammad ibn Yusuf informed us, Muhammad ibn Isma'il narrated to us, Adam ibn Abi Iyas informed us, Ibn Abi Dhi'b informed us, Yazid ibn Abd Allah ibn Qusayt informed us from Ata' ibn Yasar from Zayd ibn Thabit, who said: I recited "al-Najm" to the Prophet (ﷺ), and he did not prostrate in it. [[Narrated by al-Bukhari in the chapter on prostration of recitation, "one who recites a prostration verse and does not prostrate": 2/554, the wording being his, and by Muslim, no. (577): 1/406, and by the author in Sharh al-Sunnah: 3/310.]]

I [[In "B": the Shaykh, the Imam, may Allah have mercy on him, said.]] say: This is evidence that the prostration of recitation is not obligatory. Umar ibn al-Khattab (may Allah be pleased with him) said: "Allah did not prescribe it for us except if we wish." This is the view of al-Shafi'i and Ahmad.

Some scholars held that the prostration of recitation is obligatory upon both the reciter and the listener, and this is the view of Sufyan al-Thawri and the companions of opinion (ashab al-ra'y).
